questions.prompt: In `int x = a() + b() * c();` (C++23), what does operator precedence guarantee about runtime execution?
options: `b()` and `c()` must both execute before `a()` executes.
`a()` must execute first because reading happens left-to-right.
The result of `b() * c()` is added to `a()`, while `a()`, `b()`, and `c()` may run in any order.
The expression is undefined behavior unless parentheses are added around `b() * c()`.
questions.explanation: Operator precedence makes `*` bind tighter than `+`, building the syntax tree `a() + (b() * c())`. It does not schedule the three function calls: `a()`, `b()`, and `c()` are indeterminately sequenced and may run in any non-overlapping order.

questions.prompt: Since C++17, what does `std::cout << first() << second() << '\n';` guarantee?
options: `first()` is sequenced before `second()`, regardless of optimization level.
`first()` and `second()` are still indeterminately sequenced because `operator<<` is overloaded.
`second()` runs before `first()` because arguments bind right-to-left.
The behavior is unspecified unless `first()` and `second()` are `noexcept`.
questions.explanation: C++17 made `E1 << E2` sequence `E1` before `E2`, and `[over.match.oper]/2` applies that built-in sequencing rule to overloaded operator syntax as well. Therefore `std::cout << first()` completes before `second()` starts.

questions.prompt: Consider a type `Flag` with an overloaded `operator&&`. When evaluating `left() && right()`, what happens if `left()` returns `Flag{false}`?
options: `right()` is skipped due to short-circuit evaluation.
`right()` still executes because overloaded `operator&&` is a function call without short-circuiting.
`right()` may execute before `left()` because function arguments are unsequenced.
The program is ill-formed because overloading `operator&&` is forbidden since C++17.
questions.explanation: Overloaded `operator&&` is dispatched as a regular function call, so both argument expressions (`left()` and `right()`) must be evaluated before the function body starts—short-circuiting is lost. Meanwhile, `[over.match.oper]/2` still sequences `left()` before `right()`.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what is true about `consume(std::shared_ptr<Widget>(new Widget{1}), compute());` if `compute()` can throw?
options: It can leak `Widget` if `compute()` runs between `new Widget{1}` and the `shared_ptr` constructor.
Argument 1 is guaranteed to finish before `compute()` is called.
`compute()` is guaranteed to run before `new Widget{1}`.
No leak occurs because argument evaluations cannot interleave, though `compute()` and argument 1 may run in either order.
questions.explanation: Since C++17, function argument expressions are indeterminately sequenced rather than unsequenced (`[expr.call]/7`). Neither argument can interleave with the other—preventing the pre-C++17 leak—but the compiler may still evaluate argument 1 first or `compute()` first.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what does `pick_lhs(a) = make_rhs();` print when `Target` defines `operator=`?
options: `lhs rhs assign ` because member calls evaluate their left object before arguments.
`rhs lhs assign ` because operator-syntax assignment sequences the right operand before the left.
Either `lhs rhs assign ` or `rhs lhs assign ` because the order is unspecified.
Undefined behavior because `pick_lhs` and `make_rhs` are unsequenced.
questions.explanation: In `[expr.ass]/1`, the right operand of an assignment is sequenced before the left operand. Under `[over.match.oper]/2`, expressions written with operator syntax (`pick_lhs(a) = make_rhs()`) preserve the built-in operator's operand sequencing rather than member-call order.

questions.prompt: Under C++23 rules, what is the behavior of `int i = 0; int v[2] = {10, 20}; v[i] = i++;`?
options: Well-defined: sets `v[1] = 0` and leaves `i == 1`.
Undefined behavior because `i` is modified and read unsequenced.
Well-defined: sets `v[0] = 0` and leaves `i == 1`.
Unspecified whether `v[0]` or `v[1]` receives `0`.
questions.explanation: While `v[i] = i++;` was undefined behavior in C++14, C++17 `[expr.ass]/1` sequenced the right operand (`i++`, yielding `0` and incrementing `i` to `1`) completely before the left operand (`v[i]`). Thus `v[1]` is assigned `0` and `i` becomes `1`.
